E1658.summary: A union that, Atwood says, man can neither cement nor increase by his own power.
E1658.body: Atwood says man can “neither cement the spiritual union or give it increase” [III.4 ¶20].

E1659.summary: Expression in a passage quoted from Helvetius, whose 'Abyss' is disclosed most inwardly, at the centre where the mystery is found.
E1659.body: In a passage Atwood quotes from Helvetius: “There, within most intimately, the Abyss of the Spoagyric artifice is disclosed” [III.1 ¶70]. The text does not explain the expression further.

E1660.summary: Church Father Atwood cites for a work's authenticity, for the Church's adoption of the Mysteries' language and rites, and for three modes of human vision.
E1660.body: Atwood cites him as mentioning a certain work without doubting its authenticity, although he judged it “instinctu fallacies spiritus” (ours: by prompting of a deceiving spirit); Atwood attributes that judgment probably to the popular notion and thinks he might later have revised it [I.1 ¶11, I.1 n12]. As St. Augustin he mentions an inextinguishable lamp consecrated to Venus [I.1 ¶18]. She names him among the Church Fathers who adopted the language and rites of the Mysteries, and notes that he quotes many lost Neoplatonist books [II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶9]. He supports her account of three modes of human vision, the third (anagogic) being placed in Elysium [II.4 ¶15].

E1661.summary: The Evangelist, cited by Atwood for the Word as Life and Light, for Christ as the Word of Life manifested, and as a practitioner of the Occult Art.
E1661.body: From the first chapter of his Gospel Atwood takes the Word/Light shining in darkness as the same Light: “In Him was Life; and the Life was the Light of men.” [II.3 ¶54, II.3 n60], and also the power to become sons of God [II.3 ¶55]. From the First Epistle she takes Christ as the Word of Life made manifest, the one awaited by prophets and philosophers: “That which was from the Beginning, which they had heard, and seen with their eyes” [IV.2 ¶15, IV.2 n10]. As St John, the Evangelist Apostle, he is cited as practising the Occult Art for the poor, healing and making gold, silver and gems; St Victor's commentary relates the particulars [I.1 ¶24]. See also St John’s Gospel.

E1662.summary: The Gospel, cited by Atwood for those to whom the Word of God came being called gods, and for the True Light perfected in the Saviour.
E1662.body: Atwood cites chapter 10 for the point that those to whom the Word of God came are called gods, set against unbelief: “thou blasphemest, because I said I am the Son of God” [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n37]. She also cites it for the True Light perfected in the Saviour, whose ray cleanses life: “The True Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world” [IV.2 ¶19, IV.2 n17].

E1663.summary: Cited by Atwood to illustrate baptism by Water set against baptism by the Holy Ghost and Fire.
E1663.body: Atwood cites him to illustrate baptism by Water versus baptism by the Holy Ghost and Fire, with the purging of the floor and burning of the chaff: “He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with Fire” [IV.2 ¶15, IV.2 n11].

E1664.summary: Cited often by Atwood, chiefly in the Appendix, for the body as temple, the marriage-union of man and God, regeneration, and the purity of the Art.
E1664.body:
In the main text Atwood cites 1 Cor. 10:1-4 on the Fathers baptized in cloud and sea, eating spiritual meat and drinking from the spiritual rock, “and that rock was Christ”, without stating its application [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n40]; the Epistle to the Hebrews, for revelation in the Son surpassing every earlier revelation of the Light: “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in times past unto the Fathers by the prophets” [IV.2 ¶17, IV.2 n10, IV.2 n13]; and his saying that the impurity lies in the accuser's thought, not in the Art: “to him that esteems a thing unclean, as St Paul says, it is unclean” [IV.4 ¶24].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he supports the body as a temple of the Holy Ghost, its members a laboratory for the spirit [APP ¶16]; hints at the marriage-union between man and God in Christ [APP ¶79]; and his Epistles are said to be better understood in the atmosphere of the higher Mystics than through professed commentators [APP ¶118]. Atwood reads “the letter killeth” as meaning the living letter of the law is too powerful a test for man's spirit [APP ¶143], and takes “It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption” as the law of regeneration of the anima media, seed of spirit growing to spirit [APP ¶147].

E1665.summary: Author of a commentary that, Atwood says, relates the particulars of St John's practice of the Occult Art.
E1665.body: Atwood cites a commentary by St Victor as relating the particulars of St John's practice (healing and making gold, silver and gems for the poor) [I.1 ¶24].

E1667.summary: Author of Pyrotechny Asserted, cited as testifying that Philalethes possessed the White and Red elixir and recounting his own wasteful projection.
E1667.body: In a footnote Atwood cites Starkey's Pyrotechny Asserted as eyewitness testimony (“I saw”) that Philalethes possessed the White and Red elixir, together with Starkey's account of his own wasteful projection [I.1 ¶73, I.1 n93].

E1668.summary: A name Cosmopolite, as reported by Eudoxus, gives to the Mercury, alongside 'lodestone'.
E1668.body: Eudoxus reports that Cosmopolite calls the Mercury (Our Old Man) by other names, “to which he gives also the name of steel and of the lodestone” [IV.3 ¶10]. Whether the term 'Chalybes' is the same name the text does not state.

E1669.summary: Preserver of an ancient record that Atwood cites for the conformity between death and initiation into the Grand Mysteries.
E1669.body: Atwood cites an ancient record preserved by Stoboeus for the conformity of death and initiation and its stages: “The mind is affected and agitated in death, just as it is in initiation into the Grand Mysteries.” [II.3 ¶37].

E1670.summary: The object and perfected product of the Art: for Atwood, the concentrated, fermented Ether or Light of nature, a real entity of spiritual generation, and the soul in its perfection.
E1670.body:
**Atwood's account.** The Stone is the perfective product of the Art, made in and by the universal spirit; “this very permanent water is the stone, but whilst it is water it is no stone” [I.2 ¶26, I.2 ¶29]. It is the purified, concentrated Ether perfected by its own Light — “their stone is nothing more or less than the pure Ethereality of nature” — and transmutes by assimilating crude life into its own light; she quotes “Lapis noster, hic est ignis, ex igne creatus” (ours: our stone, this is fire, created from fire) [I.2 ¶44], and calls it “this fermented Spirit or Stone” [I.2 ¶48]; the adept calls the seed of gold “the Stone of Fire” [I.2 ¶44]. It is “one mineral spirit, exalted by fermentation intrinsically in its proper kind” [I.3 n55]; “By the term Botri is here signified the Philosopher’s Stone” [I.3 n52]. Hidden in the interior of the 'earth', it is “the true medicine” [II.3 ¶29]; it comes and is generated with Light, then brings forth clouds and darkness [II.3 ¶30, III.1 ¶49]; its most abstruse principle is the Salt of Saturn (voice unclear) [II.3 ¶41]; the armament contends “for the self-same Stone” [III.1 ¶68], its mother being the secret menstrual (after Eirenaeus) and its Quintessence the soul (after Synesius) [III.1 ¶69]; made in the furnace with 'our glass', it is “a new hypostasis, and a new stone”, “that renowned Terra Maga in aethere clarificata”, and “the Stone with the new name written in the Revelation” [II.3 ¶52, II.3 ¶54]. What the philosophers found is “this miraculous principle of regeneration” [III.1 ¶50]. Only one unclean thing enters its composition; purged after its darkness it becomes a white Elixir [III.1 ¶61]. It is “a pure petrification of the Spirit” [IV.1 ¶29], the concentrated virtue of the Universal Subject, and “the transmutative ferment” = Form of Gold = ray of motive Light [IV.4 ¶2, IV.4 ¶9]; once fermented it coequals itself to all, “the universal medium of restoration and preservation” [IV.3 ¶27, IV.3 ¶28]. The Hermetic method and its end are “the true Christian Philosopher’s Stone” [IV.3 ¶62]; the regenerate soul puts on its crown of light as a new body [IV.4 ¶20].

In the Appendix (later layer) it is “the efflux of such a life, drawn to a focus and made manifest as a concrete Essence of Light” [APP ¶6]; “a real entity produced by spiritual generation”, “a real ens of light” [APP ¶93]; “a metaphysico-chemical birth” [APP ¶108]; life in its petrified first state, to be taken and fermented [APP ¶132]; analogue of the Chief Corner Stone [APP ¶139]; and “The soul in its perfection is the Christian philosopher’s stone.” [APP ¶181].

**Quoted voices.** Geber and the monk of the Rosary: “The Stone is one”; “our Stone is no other than a foetant spirit and living water” [I.2 ¶11]. Hermes: “the concealed Stone of many colours; which is born in one colour” [I.3 ¶13]; composed from four elements [I.3 ¶26]; “the most precious gold without spots”, the Universal Ferment [I.3 ¶60]. The adepts: “a true mineral petrification” [I.3 n13], with many cover names (the feminine of magnesia, the hen, the white spittle, the volatile milk, the incombustible ash) but one epithet, the Philosopher's Stone [I.3 ¶11]. Old Alchemists: “this vapour is the Stone known and proven in the Book of Life” [III.2 ¶7]. Khunrath: a glorified King, “a shining carbuncle” [III.3 ¶19]. The adeptest: it is “Ruach Elohim, which moved upon the face of the waters” [III.3 ¶50]. Maier: “et habebis lapidem philosophorum” (ours: and you will have the philosophers' stone) [III.3 ¶31]. Arnold: dissolve it “in its own mercury” [IV.1 ¶7]. Norton/Bloomfield: “The Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral Stone.” [IV.2 ¶36]. Eudoxus: formed “by the conjunction of the spirit with the body”, “the Sea of the Wise”, “an Astral Fire”, and, after Hermes, “the vine of the Wise” [IV.3 ¶3, IV.3 ¶5, IV.3 ¶16]. Flamel: perfected, it transmutes metals and removes the root of sin from its maker [I.1 ¶57]. The theosophist: “Herein the Philosophers’ Stone or tincture lyeth.” [IV.3 ¶38].

**History.** Treatises on it are ascribed to Aristotle, the Alexandrian adepts and Artephius [I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶27]; it was never found when sought “from selfish motives and a blind love of gain” [I.1 ¶39]; Ripley sought it in vain with common substances [I.1 ¶65]; Van Helmont says “I have seen the Stone and handled it” [I.1 ¶76].

E1671.summary: Heading under which readers filed an unattributed Latin saying attached to the summary that the Art consists in an association of the Spirit.
E1671.body: An unattributed Latin saying, “Ut ventus qui fiat est ille qui dat. --- Qui capit ille sapit.” (ours, roughly: as the wind that blows is the one that gives; who grasps it is wise), is attached to the summary that the Art consists in an association of the Spirit [I.3 n59]. Elsewhere an adept calls the seed of gold “the Stone of Fire” (see Stone) [I.2 ¶44].

E1672.summary: Atwood's name for the product of the work: the perfected lowest life, completed in three circulations and analogous to the Head Stone of the Corner.
E1672.body: Atwood says “the Stone of the Wise is the perfected lowest life, its true consummation”, mineral in origin and analogous to Christ the Head Corner Stone [APP ¶46, Appendix layer]. Raised up by the builders while each in turn rejects it, it becomes the Head Stone of the Corner, “as the Stone of the Wise is completed in three successive circulations” [IV.2 ¶33]. See Stone.

E1673.summary: A tale Atwood cites to illustrate that wickedness bars approach to the material of the Art.
E1673.body: Atwood cites “the story of an Arabian Magician, who must needs steal a little boy” to illustrate that wickedness bars approach to the material [III.4 ¶6].

E1674.summary: Cited by Atwood in support of the view that philosophy was the object of the Eleusinian rites.
E1674.body: Atwood cites Strabo in support of philosophy being the object of the Eleusinian rites [II.2 ¶5].

E1675.summary: The material the Art works on, never openly declared by the adepts; something the student must find that reciprocates the design, without which the work stays abortive.
E1675.body: Atwood calls it “even the common Subject of their Art”, which the adepts never openly declare [I.1 ¶82]. One may be “really conversant with the Subject” [III.4 ¶7]. To begin operations the student needs it: “without a Subject to work with and reciprocate the design it remains abortive” [III.4 ¶29]; she discusses it as 'suitable assistance'. The text does not define it further in these passages.

E1676.summary: What unassisted reason fails to grasp, eluding the mind as it pursues it.
E1676.body: Atwood says “the Subject Identity slides evermore behind the retardant mind” — reason alone cannot grasp it [II.1 ¶32].

E1677.summary: What the work is performed on, constantly concealed by the adepts; also what underlies a species, corruptible and transferable, identified with the metals' radical moisture.
E1677.body: Atwood notes that even candid texts such as Norton's Ordinal conceal it: “with the exception of the Subject Matter and certain preliminaries, which are constantly concealed” [I.1 ¶64]. In a second sense it is what underlies a species: not species, “but the Subjects of species rather, since they are corruptible and may be changed”, so it can be freed and transferred to another form [I.2 ¶5]; of the metals she speaks of “the subject-matter of these metals, the radical moisture of which they are uniformly composed” [I.2 ¶4].

E1678.summary: In a summary from Plotinus and Porphyry that Atwood endorses: what persists through all change of bodies, receiving and reflecting forms; matter subsists according to it.
E1678.body: In a summary gathered from Plotinus and Porphyry, endorsed by Atwood, it is distinct from bodies and persists through all their changes: “that which receives the forms and reflects them --- always remains the same” [III.2 ¶47]. Matter is spoken of “according to the subject which is indefinite, because it is note form” [III.2 ¶49].

E1679.summary: The soul that suffers when pressed by evil and must be filled by a superior or an inferior power.
E1679.body: Atwood asks: “And what will not the subject soul suffer when pressed by so execrable an evil?” — such a soul must be filled by a superior or an inferior power [III.4 ¶6]. The sense of 'subject' here is left open.

E1680.summary: In an unattributed saying, the matter pierced by Divine Light, in which the pattern of the universe appears as in a glass.
E1680.body: Quoted with 'it is said': when Divine Light pierces their bosom, “the pattern of the whole universe appears in those Subject Waters, as an image in a glass” [III.3 ¶39].

E1681.summary: The cause of mesmerism's own effects, which, Atwood says, mesmerism has not investigated.
E1681.body: Atwood faults mesmerism for not investigating “the subject-being, the cause of its own effects” [II.2 ¶7].

E1682.summary: The product the Alchemists made sublime by an actual subversion of the selfhood.
E1682.body: Atwood says that by actual subversion of the selfhood “they made their Sublimate sublime” [IV.1 ¶47].

E1683.summary: The raising of the Spirit through degrees of concentrated essentiality; an operation that volatilizes and washes it and separates subtle from gross parts.
E1683.body: For Atwood, by grafting and transplanting “a growth and sublimation of the Spirit was effected, even to a third, fourth, and fifth degree of concentrated essentiality” [III.1 ¶9]; “sublimation volatilizes and washes it” [III.2 ¶64]. Vaughan speaks of “a first and second sublimation”, needed for the Matter to be alterable, without explaining them [IV.2 ¶35]. Eudoxus defines it as separating the Elements by “raising up the subtle and pure parts above the thick and terrestrial parts”, and says “Without the sublimation of the Stone, the conversion of the Elements and the extraction of the Principles is impossible” [IV.3 ¶5].

E1684.summary: The unity of all that is: fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law, and source of miracles and every natural and supernatural increase.
E1684.body: Atwood calls it “the Substant Unity of all that is; the fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law”, “the source of so many miracles and magical accordances, as of every natural and supernatural increase” [III.3 ¶79].

E1685.summary: The extracted product, seminally equal to the whole of its parts; identified with the dry splendour and the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine.
E1685.body: Atwood speaks of “that Subtendent which is found seminally equal to the whole of the parts whence it is derived”, and identifies it with the dry splendour: “this is that Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine before alluded to, and that Subtendent” [III.3 ¶71].

E1686.summary: A nature pervading the universe, the All in everything, and alterable by art throughout.
E1686.body: Atwood speaks of “a Subtle Nature pervading the universe, which is the All in every thing and susceptible of artificial alteration through all” [IV.4 ¶12].

E1687.summary: The fullness Matter and other things reach through desire of the Good, in which they become tranquil, freed from parturitions and natural desire.
E1687.body: In a passage whose voice is unclear, things reach this fullness through desire of the Good: “when things have run up so far as to this Sufficience they become tranquil in it”, freed from parturitions and natural desire [III.4 ¶28].

E1688.summary: Cited for dating Hermes before the Pharaohs, for defining Chimia, and for the Emperor's burning of Egyptian chemical books.
E1688.body: Atwood cites Suidas for placing Hermes before the Pharoahs, about 400 years before Moses, and for his entry on Chemeia: “Chimia est auri et argenti confectio” (ours: Chimia is the making of gold and silver) [I.1 ¶6, I.1 n6, I.1 n8]. He also supports her account of the Emperor burning chemical books because the Egyptians made gold and silver, which she uses to explain antiquity's silence about the Egyptian Art [I.1 ¶18, I.1 n24].
